# Supply and Demand

## Demand

In this part of the lecture we look at the buyer's side of the market. Demand is the quantity of a good that consumers are willing and able to buy at each possible price during a given period. Willingness alone is not enough; a buyer must also have the money to pay. Many students mix up demand with the quantity demanded, so read this section twice.

### The Law of Demand

When the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, other things equal. Economists explain this with the substitution effect and the income effect. A higher price makes other goods relatively cheaper, so buyers switch to them. The demand curve therefore slopes downward from left to right.

### Shifts in Demand

A change in price moves buyers along the demand curve, but a change in any other factor shifts the whole curve. The main shifters are income, the prices of related goods, tastes, expectations and the number of buyers. For a normal good, higher income increases demand; for an inferior good, higher income decreases it. Substitutes, such as tea and coffee, move together: if coffee becomes more expensive, demand for tea rises. We will see many examples of this in the seminar.

## Supply

Let us now turn to sellers. Supply is the quantity of a good that producers are willing and able to sell at each possible price. Producers respond to profit, and profit depends on price and cost.

### The Law of Supply

As the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises, other things equal. A higher price covers the higher marginal cost of producing extra units. The supply curve slopes upward. Input prices, technology, taxes and the number of sellers shift the supply curve.

## Market Equilibrium

Markets bring buyers and sellers together. The equilibrium price is the price at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied. At this price the market clears and there is no pressure for the price to change. This idea goes back to Alfred Marshall, who drew the famous scissors diagram in 1890.

### Shortages and Surpluses

Below the equilibrium price, the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied, which creates a shortage. Sellers then raise prices until the shortage disappears. Above the equilibrium price a surplus appears, and sellers cut prices to get rid of unsold stock. Price ceilings set below equilibrium cause lasting shortages, as rent control often shows.

## Elasticity

Elasticity measures how strongly one variable responds to a change in another. The price elasticity of demand equals the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. Demand is elastic when this value is greater than 1 and inelastic when it is less than 1. Goods with few substitutes, like insulin, have inelastic demand. Remember to use absolute values in exam answers.
